newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends firmer vs yen, lower vs mark in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends firmer vs yen, lower vs mark in U.S..

text.p: The dollar finished firmer versus the yen but weaker against the mark on Friday as traders squared their books and the German unit gained against a broad array of currencies, experts said.
Market participants played down rumors that some European central banks, the Federal Reserve or the Bank of Japan were buying dollars for yen.
This talk of central bank intervention to bolster the dollar emerged at the end of a week in which the dollar tumbled to 114.70 yen, its lowest level in more than four months.
The dollar dipped briefly to 114.87 yen on Friday then rebounded to close at 115.65/75 yen, up from 115.35/45 at the open.

"They've been selling all week. It's just squaring up here," said Robert Ryan, manager of corporate foreign exchange at the Bank of New York. "I think it's just been a very long week and everyone's slowing down."
Against the mark, the dollar ended at 1.6920/30, down from 1.7000/05.
The mark increased in value relative to the yen as well as the Italian lira, French franc, and British pound on Friday.
The mark traded near 68.33/36 yen in late dealings, up from around 67.95/99 in mid morning activity.
Analysts said mark gains against these currencies helped boost it against the dollar.

Mark gains versus the European currencies came just one day after German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told parliament that tax revenues for 1997 would be 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) less than expected
This shortfall could hinder Germany's efforts to qualify for the proposed single European currency or European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Part of the reason why the mark strengthened "may have to do with the issue of the tax shortfall and some concern over EMU in general. And obviously that raises the spectre of it getting delayed or not happening at all," said David Solin, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
Solin also attributed mark gains against the other European currencies to profit taking ahead of a holiday on Monday.
Financial markets in many European countries will be closed for the Whit Monday holiday.

On Tuesday, the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets to debate whether to increase short-term interest rates or leave them unchanged. The federal funds rate was hiked by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25.
Market participants were divided over what the central bank will decide to do.

"I'd say the market is split on the Fed fifty-fifty," said Marc Chandler, a senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "I don't see data before now and the FOMC meeting that is...going to fundamentally change that."
Chandlers said the housing data was not all that important because it did not change the perception that the economy is relatively robust.

The Commerce Department reported that housing starts rose 2.6 percent in April to a 1.473 million unit annualized rate. Economists polled by Reuters had expected starts at a 1.43 million annualized rate.

Elsewhere, the dollar fell to 1.4195/05 Swiss francs from 1.4280/90, but rose to Canadian $1.3730/35 from C$1.3669/74. Sterling slid to $1.6360/70 from $1.6390/00. The Australian dollar climbed to $0.7760/65 from $0.7749/54.
